title: Hearing Aid Clinics
one_liner: Hearing aid clinics sell, fit and service prescription hearing aids, with demand anchored by an aging population and challenged by OTC and consumer-electronics alternatives.
overview: Hearing aid clinics generate revenue by testing patients, recommending devices, fitting and programming hearing aids, selling batteries and accessories, and providing repairs, warranties and follow-up adjustments. The 2021 baseline described a $2.5 billion 2020 industry that was recovering from COVID-19 disruption and forecast to reach roughly $2.7 billion by 2025. Current 2025-2026 evidence points to a larger hearing-care opportunity than the clinic-only revenue pool: the US hearing aids market was estimated at $5.47 billion in 2025 by Fortune Business Insights, while Grand View Research estimated the US hearing aids device market at $2.395 billion in 2025. Clinics remain central for prescription and complex fittings, but OTC hearing aids, Costco-style value retail, tele-audiology and Apple’s FDA-authorized hearing-aid software are expanding lower-cost channels.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US hearing aid clinic/store revenue: about $2.7 billion; 2025 broader US hearing aids market: $5.47 billion including devices and implants; 2025 US hearing aids device market: $2.395 billion
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025 clinic revenue baseline forecast CAGR: 1.8%; 2025-2032 broader US hearing aids market forecast CAGR: 11.3%; 2026-2035 US hearing aids device market forecast CAGR: 6.6%
key_stats.older_population: 2025 US population age 65+: 64.6 million, up 16.2% from April 1, 2020
key_stats.otc_market: 2025 US OTC hearing aids market: $272.1 million; 2026 projected: $310.6 million; 2026-2035 CAGR: 9.3%
key_stats.adoption: 2025 MarkeTrak hearing aid adoption among people with hearing difficulty: 39.0%, including 33.5% traditional hearing aids and 5.7% OTC hearing aids
key_stats.professional_workforce: 2025 US median wage for hearing aid specialists: $65,160; 2024 audiologist employment: 15,800 with 2024-2034 projected growth of 9%

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated clinic revenue: about $2.56 billion, derived from the baseline report’s 2020 revenue of $2.469 billion and 2020-2026 projected CAGR of 1.77%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline trajectory: about 1.8% annual revenue growth after the 2020 COVID-19 decline; baseline forecast was $2.7 billion by 2025
baseline_2022.revenue_mix: 2020 baseline: digital hearing aids 50.0% of revenue, analog hearing aids 33.0%, batteries and accessories 14.8%, other services 2.2%
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2020 baseline EBIT profit margin: 10.7%; 2025 baseline forecast margin: 12.9%

how_it_makes_money: Clinics earn from bundled hearing aid sales, professional hearing evaluations, device fitting and programming, warranties, batteries, accessories, cleaning, repairs, follow-up visits and replacement cycles. Most revenue is tied to prescription device dispensing, where the clinic margin is supported by counseling, customization, trial-period management and ongoing service rather than the device alone.
cost_structure: The largest cost categories are hearing aid inventory and components purchased from manufacturers, wages for audiologists, hearing instrument specialists and front-office staff, rent for local clinic footprints, marketing and lead generation, insurance, software and equipment, utilities, repairs and warranty fulfillment. Baseline 2020 profit was 10.7% of revenue, with margin recovering toward 12.9% by 2025 as in-person volume normalized and larger retail networks gained purchasing leverage.
major_players: Sonova Holding AG / Phonak / Connect Hearing
GN Store Nord / Beltone / ReSound / Jabra Enhance
Audicus, Eargo, MDHearing and other direct-to-consumer or OTC brands
current_dynamics: Demand is supported by the 2025 US 65+ population of 64.6 million, low historical treatment penetration and growing hearing-health awareness. Medicare still does not cover hearing aids under Original Medicare in 2026, but Medicare Advantage plans broadly offer hearing benefits, creating managed-network opportunities and pricing constraints. OTC devices have not displaced professional care for many users because fitting, counseling and returns remain pain points, but they have expanded the entry-level market and trained consumers to compare clinic pricing. AI-enabled sound processing, Bluetooth streaming, rechargeable batteries, remote fittings and app-based adjustments are increasingly table stakes.
whats_growing: Receiver-in-the-ear and digital devices, rechargeable models, AI-assisted speech-in-noise processing, tele-audiology, remote adjustments, Medicare Advantage network volume, OTC self-fitting devices, Costco and warehouse-club hearing centers, and consumer-electronics hearing features are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Analog hearing aid sales, battery-only accessory dependence as rechargeable models spread, standalone high-price clinic models with opaque bundled pricing, COVID-era deferred-care backlog, and simple mild-to-moderate cases that do not require professional fitting are shrinking as a share of demand.
recent_developments: 2022-10-17: FDA OTC hearing aid rules took effect, allowing adults with perceived mild-to-moderate hearing loss to buy qualifying devices without a prescription or audiologist visit.
2024-09-12: FDA authorized Apple’s AirPods Pro 2 Hearing Aid Feature as the first OTC hearing aid software device.
2025-03-28: Fortune Business Insights estimated the US hearing aids market at $5.47 billion in 2025 and forecast 11.3% CAGR through 2032.
2025-06-26: Census reported the US population age 65+ reached 61.2 million in 2024, up 3.1% from 2023; the Vintage 2025 release later put 65+ at 64.6 million in 2025.
2025-08-13: MarkeTrak 2025 reported hearing aid adoption at 39.0%, with OTC devices accounting for 5.7% adoption among people with hearing difficulty.
2026-02-01: Global Market Insights estimated the US OTC hearing aids market at $272.1 million in 2025 and projected $310.6 million for 2026.
outlook: The clinic channel should keep growing through 2026 because age-driven need and better awareness outweigh substitution in complex and moderate-to-severe cases. Growth will likely be slower than the broader device market because OTC, online and warehouse channels capture price-sensitive and first-time mild-loss consumers. The strongest clinics will compete on diagnostics, counseling, transparent pricing, insurance navigation, recurring service and hybrid remote support, while weaker independents face consolidation pressure from manufacturer-owned chains, national retailers and lead-generation platforms.
one_sentence: The US Hearing Aid Clinics industry remains a modest-growth, service-heavy healthcare retail niche where demographics and Medicare Advantage hearing benefits support demand, while OTC devices, warehouse clubs, online sellers and AI-enabled earbuds pressure pricing and shift simpler cases away from traditional clinic visits.

title: Heating & Air Conditioning Equipment Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US HVACR equipment manufacturers are benefiting from commercial HVAC, data center cooling and replacement demand, while residential softness, A2L refrigerant conversion and metal tariffs pressure volumes and costs.
overview: This industry manufactures residential, commercial and industrial HVACR equipment, including central air conditioners, heat pumps, warm-air furnaces, rooftop units, chillers, air handlers, commercial refrigeration systems, coils, controls and related components. The 2022 IBIS baseline showed revenue of $55.7B and 2022 growth of 7.4% after the 2020 pandemic decline. Current public Census M3 data for ventilation, heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment manufacturing show shipments of $71.8B in 2025, up 10.3% from 2024, and $39.3B in H1 2026, up 9.8% from H1 2025. Growth is being pulled by commercial HVAC, retrofit work, energy-efficiency replacement, low-GWP refrigerant redesigns and data center cooling, while high interest rates, softer residential construction, distributor destocking and input-cost volatility are restraining unit volumes.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 manufacturers' value of shipments for ventilation, heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment was $71.8B, up from $65.1B in 2024 and $59.3B in 2023.
key_stats.growth: 2025 shipments grew 10.3% year over year after 2024 growth of 9.7% and 2023 growth of 7.8%.
key_stats.latest_run_rate: H1 2026 shipments were $39.3B, up 9.8% from H1 2025.
key_stats.baseline_profit_margin: IBISWorld baseline profit margin was 6.9% in 2022.
key_stats.baseline_employment: IBISWorld baseline employment was 148,487 workers in 2022.
key_stats.baseline_imports_exports: IBISWorld baseline imports were $25.9B in 2022 and exports were $7.2B in 2022.
key_stats.shipments_mix_signal: AHRI data showed 2024 US shipments of 5.560M central air conditioners, 4.122M air-source heat pumps and 3.151M warm-air furnaces; 2025 heat pump shipments were reported at 3.64M versus 3.25M gas warm-air furnaces.

baseline_2022.market_size: IBISWorld revenue was $55.7B in 2022, in 2022 dollars.
baseline_2022.growth: IBISWorld estimated 2022 revenue growth of 7.4% and 2017-2022 CAGR of 2.5%.
baseline_2022.profit: IBISWorld profit was $3.8B in 2022, equal to a 6.9% margin.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell equipment and components to HVAC contractors, distributors, builders, commercial building owners, industrial customers, retailers and refrigeration wholesalers. Revenue comes from factory-built systems such as split AC units, heat pumps, rooftop units, furnaces, chillers, air handlers, commercial refrigerators, walk-in systems, coils, controls, parts and selected repair or contract manufacturing receipts. Higher-margin revenue is increasingly tied to engineered commercial systems, data center cooling, controls, aftermarket parts and efficiency-driven replacement cycles rather than only commodity residential units.
cost_structure: Major costs are metals, compressors, coils, motors, electronics, refrigerants, factory labor, logistics, warranty expense, R&D and regulatory compliance. IBISWorld reported 2022 profit at 6.9% of revenue and 2022 wages of $8.8B. In 2025-2026, A2L refrigerant redesign, R-454B cylinder constraints, steel and aluminum tariffs, copper exposure and inventory conversion costs increased working-capital and pricing pressure, while larger commercial HVAC players used price realization and productivity programs to protect margins.

current_dynamics: The industry is expanding in dollars but bifurcating by end market. Commercial HVAC is strong in 2025-2026, especially applied systems, rooftop units, chillers, controls, retrofit work and data center cooling. Residential replacement remains active but more price-sensitive, while new-home demand is constrained by 2025-2026 mortgage-rate and affordability pressure. The 2025 shift from R-410A to lower-GWP A2L refrigerants pulled forward some inventory, disrupted installations and created R-454B cylinder shortages. Producer prices remain elevated, with the HVAC and commercial refrigeration equipment PPI at 239.481 in June 2026, and metal tariffs added cost uncertainty after the 2025 increase in steel and aluminum tariff rates.
whats_growing: Commercial applied HVAC and building retrofit projects in 2025-2026.
Data center liquid cooling, computer-room air conditioning and high-capacity custom air handling in 2025-2026.
Heat pumps as a share of heating equipment, with 2025 heat pump shipments reported above 2025 gas warm-air furnace shipments.
Low-GWP A2L-compatible systems after the January 1, 2025 residential and light commercial compliance date.
Aftermarket parts, service-linked controls and efficiency upgrades in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: R-410A residential and light commercial equipment manufacturing after the January 1, 2025 transition deadline for new equipment.
Commodity residential HVAC unit volumes in 2025 where high rates, destocking and consumer affordability weighed on replacements.
Gas warm-air furnace demand relative to heat pumps, with 2025 heat pump shipments reported at 3.64M versus 2025 gas furnace shipments of 3.25M.
Older low-efficiency systems as DOE efficiency rules and utility incentives support replacement.
Margin room for smaller manufacturers in 2025-2026 as refrigerant, metal and logistics costs stay volatile.
recent_developments: 2025-01-01: EPA Technology Transitions restrictions began for many residential and light commercial AC and heat pump products using higher-GWP HFCs.
2025-06-04: US steel and aluminum tariff rates increased to 50% for covered articles and derivative articles, raising cost risk for HVAC cabinets, coils and components.
2025-10-22: Daikin released its 2025 Business and Innovation Report highlighting expanded US manufacturing, R&D and workforce investment.
2026-01-29: Trane Technologies reported 2025 revenue of $21.3B, up 7.5%, and year-end backlog of $7.8B, up 15% from 2024.
2026-02-05: Carrier reported 2025 sales of $21.75B, down 3% from 2024, but cited double-digit growth in global commercial HVAC and aftermarket.
2026-07-15: FRED/BLS showed the HVAC and commercial refrigeration equipment PPI at 239.481 for June 2026.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but uneven. Census shipments for H1 2026 were $39.3B, up 9.8% from H1 2025, showing continued dollar growth. Commercial HVAC, data centers, electrification, low-GWP product refreshes and energy-efficiency retrofits should keep demand firm through 2026. Residential equipment is likely to lag until housing affordability improves and the A2L inventory transition normalizes. Margin performance will depend on manufacturers' ability to pass through tariff, refrigerant, copper, aluminum and steel costs while avoiding production delays from component shortages.
one_sentence: In 2025, the industry shifted from the 2022 post-pandemic rebound into a higher-dollar but more uneven cycle, with Census M3 HVAC/refrigeration equipment shipments reaching $71.8B in 2025, up 10.3% from 2024, even as residential equipment shipments weakened during the refrigerant transition.

title: Heating & Air Conditioning Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: HVAC wholesalers sit between equipment makers and contractors, with 2025 demand pressured by weak single-family starts, A2L refrigerant conversion and contractor inventory resets.
overview: Heating & Air Conditioning Wholesaling in the US is a mature, contractor-facing distribution industry. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline reported 2021 revenue of $72.4 billion and 2021 growth of 7.5%, but newer public commercial estimates use narrower HVAC-distribution boundaries, with U.S. HVAC distribution revenue at $51.0 billion in 2025 and $54.0 billion estimated for 2026. Demand softened in 2025 as single-family construction declined, central AC and heat-pump shipments fell, and distributors worked through the shift from R-410A equipment to lower-GWP A2L systems. The long-run support remains strong: aging installed equipment, hotter summers, electrification, heat-pump adoption, indoor air quality upgrades and commercial retrofit work keep replacement demand recurring even when new construction is weak.

key_stats.market_size: $51.0 billion in 2025 U.S. HVAC distribution revenue; $54.0 billion estimated for 2026 under the same commercial-source boundary
key_stats.growth: 6.39% CAGR forecast for 2026-2033 U.S. HVAC distribution revenue; 2025 AC and air-source heat-pump shipments fell 20.0% year over year to 7.75 million units
key_stats.establishments: 6,477 employer establishments in 2023 for NAICS 423730 Warm Air Heating and Air-Conditioning Equipment and Supplies Merchant Wholesalers
key_stats.housing_starts: 1.36 million U.S. housing starts in 2025, down 0.6% from 2024; single-family starts were 943,000 in 2025, down 6.9%
key_stats.leading_public_distributor: Watsco revenue was $7.24 billion in 2025, down 5.0% from 2024, with a 28.0% gross margin

baseline_2022.source_file: IBISWorld baseline file last updated February 27, 2022
baseline_2022.market_size: $72.4 billion in 2021 revenue, stated in 2021 dollars
baseline_2022.growth: 7.5% revenue growth in 2021 and 7.6% annualized revenue growth over 2016-2021
baseline_2022.outlook: $72.9 billion forecast 2026 revenue and 0.1% annualized revenue growth over 2021-2026

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers buy HVAC equipment and supplies from manufacturers, hold local inventory, provide counter sales, delivery, credit, technical support and digital ordering to contractors, then earn gross margin on equipment, replacement parts, ductwork, controls, filtration products and related supplies. Most revenue flows from residential and commercial HVAC contractors performing replacement, repair, remodel and new-build installation work.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost category; 2025 margins were shaped by OEM price increases, tariffs and A2L equipment costs.
cost_structure.wages: Important operating cost for branch, warehouse, counter-sales, technical-support and delivery staff; IBIS baseline reported $6.31 billion in 2021 wages.
cost_structure.freight_and_facilities: Branch rent, fleet, fuel, warehousing and last-mile delivery costs rose in 2025 as distributors carried transitional A2L inventory.
cost_structure.inventory_carrying_cost: Material in 2025 because distributors stocked both legacy R-410A and new A2L equipment; Watsco inventory peaked at $2.1 billion in 2025 and declined to $1.4 billion by December 31, 2025.
cost_structure.technology: Digital ordering, pricing optimization, inventory systems and contractor apps are increasingly used to defend margin and reduce service cost.
cost_structure.profit_margin: IBIS baseline profit margin was 4.2% in 2021; Watsco 2025 gross margin was 28.0%, a distributor-level gross margin rather than industry EBIT margin.

major_players: Manufacturers' captive distribution branches from Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Daikin and other OEMs
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being reset by three forces: lower residential unit volumes, the A2L refrigerant transition and pricing actions from OEMs. Housing starts were nearly flat in 2025, but single-family starts fell 6.9%, hurting new residential HVAC demand. AHRI-reported 2025 shipments of central AC and air-source heat pumps fell 20.0%, reflecting lower volumes, inventory destocking and installation disruption during the product conversion. At the same time, higher average selling prices, stricter refrigerant rules and demand for replacement equipment are supporting nominal distributor revenue and margin for scaled operators.
whats_growing: Heat pumps, A2L-compatible equipment, higher-efficiency replacement systems, smart controls, indoor-air-quality products, digital contractor ordering, commercial retrofit demand and distributor consolidation are growing. Heat pumps remained larger than gas warm-air furnace shipments in 2025, with 3.64 million heat pumps shipped versus 3.25 million gas warm-air furnaces.
whats_shrinking: Legacy R-410A equipment availability, central AC unit shipments, single-family new-construction demand, smaller independent distributor share and excess transition inventory are shrinking. 2025 AC-only shipments fell 26.2% to 4.10 million units, while Watsco reported a 7.0% decline in HVAC equipment sales for 2025.
recent_developments: 2025-01-01: EPA Technology Transitions restrictions began for many higher-GWP HFC residential and light-commercial AC and heat-pump products, accelerating A2L equipment conversion.
2025-09-30: EPA proposed reforms to extend some HFC compliance deadlines, including residential air conditioning and refrigeration subsectors.
2026-02-13: AHRI year-end 2025 data showed AC and air-source heat-pump shipments down 20.0% to 7.75 million units.
2026-02-17: Watsco reported 2025 revenue of $7.24 billion, down 5.0%, and record 2025 gross margin of 28.0% after the A2L transition and inventory reduction.
2026-02-18: NAHB reported 2025 housing starts of 1.36 million, down 0.6%, with single-family starts down 6.9% to 943,000.
2026-03-23: EPA updated refrigerant sales-restriction guidance, reiterating wholesaler invoice-retention and certified-technician requirements.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously improving but uneven. Public commercial forecasts put U.S. HVAC distribution revenue at $54.0 billion in 2026 and project 6.39% annual growth through 2033. Replacement demand should normalize as A2L conversion disruption fades, while high rates and affordability constraints continue to cap single-family new-construction volume. Scaled distributors with broad branch networks, strong OEM access, inventory discipline and contractor-facing digital platforms are positioned to gain share from smaller independents.
one_sentence: The industry distributes central air conditioners, heat pumps, furnaces, ductwork, filtration systems and parts to HVAC contractors, so its near-term cycle is tied to replacement demand, housing starts, nonresidential construction and regulatory product transitions.

title: Heavy Duty Truck Parts Dealers
one_liner: Heavy-duty truck parts dealers distribute replacement and production parts that keep Class 7 and Class 8 commercial fleets running.
overview: Operators primarily wholesale truck parts and supplies for heavy-duty and commercial trucks, including engine parts, drivetrain components, transmissions, differentials, suspensions, cabs, exterior and structural parts, and electronics; new tires and tubes are excluded. In 2025, IBISWorld estimated industry revenue at $25.5 billion after a 2020-2025 CAGR of 2.2% and 2025 growth of 1.1%, reflecting a recovery from pandemic disruption but a still-cautious freight environment. Demand is tied to truck transportation volumes, repair and maintenance activity, truck and bus manufacturing, vehicle age, steel and parts input costs, and emissions-related equipment complexity.

how_it_makes_money: Dealers buy parts from OEMs, component manufacturers and wholesalers, hold local or regional inventory, and earn wholesale margins by selling into fleets, repair shops, truck dealers, manufacturers, auto parts stores, independent garages and service networks. Revenue is driven by replacement frequency, parts availability, delivery speed, e-commerce ordering, national account pricing, private-label or aftermarket alternatives, and value-added services such as diagnostics, shop service, technical support and inventory programs.
cost_structure: The largest 2025 cost bucket is purchased inventory, including mechanical parts, electronics, structural components and imported or domestically sourced components; margins are exposed to steel, freight, tariff and supplier pricing. Labor is a smaller but important cost because counter staff, sales teams, warehouse workers, delivery drivers and technicians support availability and service. In 2022, baseline wages were $1.411 billion, equal to about 6.7% of 2022 revenue, while baseline profit was 3.2% of revenue. In 2025, industry profit improved to 5.1%, but carriers and distributors still faced cost pressure from 2025 parts pricing increases of 4.0% and 2025 repair-and-maintenance cost inflation of 8.6%. Other costs include warehousing, local delivery fleets, rent, IT and e-commerce platforms, credit losses, insurance, and working capital tied up in broad SKU inventories.
major_players: LKQ Corporation: IBISWorld identifies LKQ as the largest company and the only named company with meaningful share on its 2025 public page.
FleetPride: a leading independent aftermarket heavy-duty parts and service distributor that merged with TruckPro in 2025.
TruckPro: merged with FleetPride in 2025 and continues as a major heavy-duty parts and service business within the combined FleetPride platform.
OEM dealer parts networks: truck OEM-affiliated dealer channels remain important for genuine OE parts, warranty-linked repairs and newer fleet sourcing.
Regional independent distributors and HDD specialists: still meaningful because the industry remains fragmented and locally service-intensive.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is split between weak freight fundamentals and durable aftermarket demand. Freight tonnage barely grew in 2025, new Class 8 sales were pressured by carrier profitability and financing costs, and smaller fleets remained cost-sensitive. At the same time, older equipment, deferred replacement, higher repair intensity, parts-price inflation, and regulatory planning for 2027 model-year standards support replacement-parts demand. The channel is consolidating, with the 2025 FleetPride-TruckPro merger strengthening national scale, while independent garages and specialist distributors benefit when aging trucks move out of warranty and buyers shift away from pure OE sourcing.
whats_growing: Heavy truck electronics, sensors, emissions controls, diagnostics-linked components, e-commerce ordering, OE-quality parts programs, private-label and aftermarket alternatives for older vehicles, national-account service models, and parts tied to brake, wheel-end, drivetrain, suspension and engine maintenance are growing. Demand is also supported by 2025 vehicle-fleet aging, 2025 aftermarket pricing increases, and 2026 Class 8 order recovery tied partly to EPA 2027 timing and improving freight rates.
whats_shrinking: Low-margin standalone local dealers without scale, slow-moving inventory, Class 7 share relative to Class 8 demand, purely manual counter-sales models, and discretionary replacement tied to weak truckload profitability are under pressure. New heavy-duty truck sales were weak in 2025 and NADA cited a 2026 Class 8 sales forecast of 171,000 units, down 18% versus 2025, which limits production-linked parts demand even as aftermarket repairs hold up.
recent_developments: 2024-03-29: EPA finalized Phase 3 greenhouse-gas standards for heavy-duty vehicles beginning with model year 2027 and extending through model year 2032.
2025-09: IBISWorld updated the US Heavy-Duty Truck Parts Dealers report and estimated 2025 revenue at $25.5 billion with 2025 growth of 1.1%.
2025-10-28: FleetPride and TruckPro announced a merger, creating a larger independent heavy-duty aftermarket parts and service distributor under the FleetPride name.
2026-01-20: ATA reported 2025 for-hire truck tonnage rose only 0.1% versus 2024, showing weak freight demand despite the first annual gain since 2022.
2026-06-23: MacKay reported 2025 medium- and heavy-duty aftermarket parts pricing rose 4.0% versus 2024, while parts availability remained the top channel challenge.
2026-07-21: ACT Research reported June 2026 North American Class 8 net orders of 31,751 units, more than triple the 2025 level, indicating recovery from depressed 2025 comparisons.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive but not broad-based. Replacement-parts demand should remain resilient because fleets are aging equipment, avoiding expensive new-truck purchases and spending more on maintenance. Revenue should benefit from 2025-2026 price inflation and improving 2026 Class 8 order momentum, but volumes remain tied to freight rates, construction, manufacturing and carrier cash flow. Over 2026-2030, consolidation, e-commerce, service bundling and technical parts expertise should favor national distributors and sophisticated regional specialists, while low-growth freight cycles, tariff and input-cost volatility, and potential rail substitution cap upside.

title: Heavy Equipment Rental in the US
one_liner: Heavy equipment rental remains a construction-cycle business, but 2025-2026 demand is being cushioned by megaprojects, infrastructure work and contractors’ preference for renting over owning costly fleet.
overview: Operators rent and lease heavy equipment such as earthmoving machines, aerial work platforms, power and HVAC systems, pumps, trench safety gear, material handling equipment and, in the broader IBIS definition, transportation-related assets. The 2022 baseline showed a post-pandemic rebound to $53.2 billion in revenue, supported by construction recovery and early federal infrastructure funding. Current 2025-2026 public data point to a larger but slower-growth market: ARA’s 2026 forecast puts combined US construction and industrial equipment plus general tool rental revenue at $83.5 billion, up 3.6% in 2026, while its late-2025 forecast placed the construction and industrial equipment component at $63.4 billion in 2025. Large public, industrial, data center, manufacturing and energy projects are offsetting weaker residential and rate-sensitive local construction demand.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is generated from daily, weekly, monthly and longer-term rentals; delivery, pickup, fuel and environmental fees; specialty rental services; re-rental of third-party fleet; maintenance and repair services; sales of used rental equipment; and smaller amounts of new equipment, parts, supplies and consumables sales. Large national accounts and megaprojects often use multi-branch fleet support, while local contractors rely on flexible rentals to avoid ownership, financing, maintenance and idle-time costs.
cost_structure: The largest costs are fleet acquisition, depreciation, maintenance, labor, delivery, fuel, insurance, branch facilities, interest expense and technology. United Rentals reported 2025 equipment-rental cost excluding depreciation of $5.888 billion and rental-equipment depreciation of $2.670 billion against $13.806 billion of equipment rental revenue. Herc reported 2025 direct operating expense of $1.602 billion and rental-equipment depreciation of $856 million against $3.770 billion of equipment rental revenue. Margin pressure in 2025 came from depreciation, delivery costs, inflation and acquisition integration costs, while scale, utilization and specialty mix supported EBITDA margins above 40% at the largest operators.
current_dynamics: The market is bifurcated in 2025-2026. Large-project demand is strong, especially infrastructure, data centers, manufacturing, energy, utilities and public works, while smaller local construction and residential work remain more exposed to interest rates and private construction softness. Contractors are renting more because equipment is expensive to finance and maintain, project timelines are uncertain and fleet flexibility matters. National chains are investing in specialty rentals, digital fleet tools and branch density, while used-equipment sales remain an important release valve for fleet mix and residual values.
whats_growing: Megaproject rentals tied to 2025-2026 infrastructure, data center, manufacturing and energy work
Specialty rentals such as trench safety, power, HVAC, pumps and industrial services, with United Rentals specialty rental revenue up 13.6% in 2025
Rental penetration, with ARA reporting the rental penetration index rose to 59.5% in 2025
Large-chain scale, with Herc completing the H&E acquisition in 2025 and guiding to $4.275 billion-$4.4 billion of equipment rental revenue in 2026
Fleet productivity at large operators, with United Rentals reporting 2.2% fleet productivity growth in 2025 and 2.9% growth for the first half of 2026
whats_shrinking: Residential construction-linked rental demand in markets affected by high financing costs, despite June 2026 housing starts improving month to month
Overall construction spending, which was down 3.2% year over year in June 2026
Lower-margin general rental work in markets without megaproject exposure
Margins where depreciation, delivery and integration costs rose faster than rental rates in 2025
Standalone midsize platforms as consolidation reduces the number of independent public rental companies
recent_developments: 2025-02-19: Herc and H&E signed a definitive merger agreement after H&E terminated its prior United Rentals deal.
2025-06-02: Herc completed its acquisition of H&E Equipment Services, adding about 160 branches across more than 30 states.
2025-11-11: ARA forecast 2025 US construction and general tool rental revenue at $80.5 billion, including $63.4 billion from construction and industrial equipment.
2026-01-28: United Rentals reported 2025 total revenue of $16.099 billion and introduced 2026 revenue guidance of $16.8 billion-$17.3 billion.
2026-05-19: ARA raised its 2026 US equipment rental forecast to $83.5 billion, up 3.6% from 2025.
2026-08-03: Census reported June 2026 construction spending at a $2.1665 trillion annual rate, down 3.2% from June 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but not broad-based. ARA’s latest 2026 forecast calls for 3.6% growth to $83.5 billion for US construction and industrial equipment plus general tool rental, followed by 3.8% growth in 2027 and 4.4% growth in 2028. Large national operators should outperform through branch density, specialty services, technology, procurement scale and megaproject exposure. Risks include weaker private construction, elevated interest rates, tariff-driven equipment inflation, utilization volatility, wage pressure and residual-value declines if fleet supply exceeds demand. The strongest growth should remain in specialty rentals, infrastructure, power, data center and manufacturing-related work, while residential and small commercial rentals are likely to lag until financing conditions improve.
one_sentence: The US heavy equipment rental industry rents construction, industrial, transportation and specialty equipment to contractors, infrastructure owners, manufacturers, utilities and other commercial customers, with demand tied to construction spending, industrial projects, fleet utilization and rental-rate discipline.
